sourceInformation.source: Densha de Go! (Taito, 1996 arcade and its home versions): the Japanese train-driving game of stopping on the mark and keeping the timetable to the second
sourceInformation.genre: Train driving simulation with arcade scoring
sourceInformation.perspective: First-person cab view (pseudo-3D rail renderer), with chase, high chase, platform and trackside cameras, a side-view Stop Cam and a top-down ring map for stage select
sourceInformation.tech: my-3D2dge v0.85.2 (full engine, handoff package) with a new rail.js pseudo-3D railway renderer forked from its ROAD module; AI Hub session client 1.4.0 (Session Protocol 1); vanilla JavaScript, no other libraries or CDN; Node 24 and Playwright 1.63.0 (Chromium) for tests and tools
sourceInformation.artDirection: The engine's PS1-era pixel style (320x240 minimum, expanded to the screen, E.tones hue-shifted shading, stepped alpha); new code-drawn trains (Halo 8000, Halo 3000, Sky Liner, freight), cab dashboards, 4-lamp signals, line-side boards, stations, a parametric Japanese townscape and hand-drawn landmarks; time-of-day colour grades, rain, fog and glare; engine Humanoid and Blob rigs for the cast and crowds
sourceInformation.animation: The engine's Humanoid and Blob rigs (idle, gait, wave, cheer) plus new bow, point and flag poses; code-tweened cab controls (the master controller, needles, lamps, wipers, sun visor), the white-gloved point-and-call hand, doors, crossing gates, the Ferris wheel and lighthouse beam, Haro-kun's squash and spinning halo, the rank stamp slam and postcard flip
sourceInformation.audio: All procedural Web Audio in code: a continuous train synth (VVVF inverter singing, resistor growl, rolling, wind, tunnel echo, bridge roar, rain, brake squeal, compressor, horn), rail-joint clicks, door chimes, the conductor's buzzer, ATS bell, crossing bells with Doppler, 12 original station departure melodies, 10 chip-music songs on the engine sequencer, and Animalese/Simlish-style gibberish voices for every character (Babble syllable synthesis with formants)
sourceInformation.online: AI Hub Session Protocol 1 in ghost mode for 2-4 players (the Parallel Run: each player on their own track, the others shown as ghost trains, live standings, the game's own card); local 2-player split-screen Duel; no other network use
sourceInformation.testing: Allowed and used: headless scripts through the engine (game.advance, input taps and holds, game.debug), a scripted playthrough of the whole game, Playwright browser checks, the AI Hub harness, screenshots for look review. One command, node test/run.mjs, runs 28 headless suites (281 checks: renderer math, route compiler, physics check values, signals and ATS, limits, stations and judgments, calls and horn, timetable calibration, scoring, crowds, events, light, cameras, HUD layout at 3 screen sizes, input and glyphs, sound, voices, story, autopilot, attract, Dev Mode and its event triggers, progress, settings, screens, a mock AI Hub, the duel, and the full playthrough) in parallel and prints only failures and a count; --browser --hub --bundle adds 72 Playwright checks on the final file (title, attract, keyboard and mouse driving, the mouse in menus, touch-only phones, PlayStation and Xbox prompts, the duel's keyboard halves, and every Dev Mode tool through its own button, the six event triggers fired at a station from the paused menu with Halo Time frozen, the sound board and the live sliders), the 3 AI Hub harness runs, and 21 checks of the deliverables against TASK.md (file name, the hub client first and unmodified, the hub tags, nothing loaded from outside, no audio or image files, the bundle current with the sources, no unfinished-work markers, this exit interview's shape)
sourceInformation.research: Read the engine handoff docs (README, API card, road module and kit, tests) and the AI Hub protocol README and examples; no web research (Densha de Go! mechanics from general knowledge)
sourceInformation.environment: Claude Code CLI (headless); Linux; browser unknown
sourceInformation.usage: API cost: unknown; tokens: unknown; session time: about 4 hours (05:02 to about 09:00 by the machine clock)

testingFeedback: How many issues did testing catch? About 42, all fixed before shipping: 23 from the headless suites and the autopilot runs (among them a scripted freight that never stopped, a standing start that could not move the train on P1, an arrival estimator that was always late and then always early, signal lookups that walked the loop in route order, grade easing that lost height, beacons not reset by a jump, a missing holding brake, comfort drained by the autopilot, a starting Halo Time that ignored the run's difficulty, an obstruction that never cleared, the HUD and tips spilling off 320 and 427 px screens, storage with no memory fallback), 15 from screenshot review (ground drawn over the ballast, a viaduct with no deck, a tunnel portal that painted the whole sky, people and lamp glows never drawn, overlapping title, results and duel layouts) and 3 from the browser checks (a menu click that only picked the focused row, Dev Mode's Skip to the next stop judging one stop and jumping past the next, and its test events firing at their scripted places instead of just ahead of the train); plus 4 mistakes in the tests themselves.

How many would be considered critical or game breaking? 8: the S2 freight deadlock (S2 could not be finished), the P1 standing start (the tutorial's first step was impossible), the plan's timetables (good drivers ran out of Halo Time), the obstruction that never cleared for a train stopped far back (S3 stuck), a name clash that crashed attract mode, a missing route helper that crashed every call, the signal lookup that skipped the terminal's restricted speed, and people and lamp glows that were never drawn.

What was the most helpful test you ran? Driving every stage headless with the autopilot and printing each event with the clock. It found the freight deadlock, the signal ordering, the timetable and scoring problems in seconds, and it grew into the scripted playthrough of the whole game.

What was the least helpful test you ran? Three early checks in the HUD and screens suites that only asserted true (I made them real later), and the first serial run of the suite, which took over 15 minutes until it was split across worker processes.
engineFeedback: What did you like most about the engine? Its headless determinism: game.advance with exact fixed steps, input taps and game.debug made a 30-minute career testable in seconds, and the Humanoid rigs, the Shell's menus and settings, and the chip synth meant a whole cast, every menu screen and all the sound needed no assets.

Did you get stuck or guess wrong? The ROAD module projects heights with half the screen height, which squashes the world on wide screens, and it has no multiple tracks, raised strips or rear cameras, so I forked it into a new renderer. I guessed the yaw for rigs drawn in my own view, assumed the Menu could scale its text (it can't, so I wrote a larger one), and did not expect E.store to have no memory fallback when localStorage is missing (headless tests, blocked storage).

What was the most important thing you had to build yourself? The rail renderer (square-pixel pseudo-3D with several tracks, strips with faces and patterns, point things, crest clipping, rear views, fog and time-of-day tinting), and on top of it the train dynamics and the model-predictive autopilot that drives attract mode, the tests and the timetable calibration.

What was the hardest part about using the engine? Finding the internals the API card does not cover (the Shell's settings rows, the audio buses, the pose solver, the Dialog's typing) in a 14,700-line file; the API index helped, but several features needed reading and patching the source.

What did you change in the engine, and why? A Dialog voice hook (per-character gibberish voices), a settings-screen group filter with Reset (Dev Mode's live sliders, hidden from the standard Settings), PlayStation glyphs by default plus face-button and menu glyphs in the font, audio bus accessors (the continuous train synth follows volume and ducking), bow, point and flag poses (staff, workers, the finale), the hub's Create+Options rule in the pad reader, and a build stamp naming this copy; plus the new rail.js module. Each is listed in ENGINE-CHANGES.md.

If you could change one thing about the engine, what would it be? Ship a general pseudo-3D strip renderer (or make ROAD square-pixel with lateral objects and rear views), because vehicle games beyond OutRun need platforms, trains and buildings beside the line.
promptFeedback: What did you like most about this prompt? It is specific about the things that matter for a real product (10-foot controller-first UI, glyph switching, attract mode, a dev mode with live sliders, the hub, one test command) and leaves the creative design open.

What was confusing? Whether Source Information should describe the plan's intentions or what was actually built, and how the plan and TASK.md title rules interact (STAGE.md says to use the plan's title, TASK.md says to pick one by RNG; the plan had already done that).

What was the hardest thing to do? Making a long, faithful career (six stages of real timetables) play well end to end and staying deterministic for tests, while also covering attract mode, local and online multiplayer, and all the front-end screens.

What would you change in this prompt? Say how long the demo should take to play, and whether a scripted full playthrough must pass on the bundle or on the dev page; and allow a shorter required career when a plan is very large.

aiHub.name: Densha de Halo!
aiHub.tagline: Stop on the mark. Leave on the second.
aiHub.description: Drive the Halo Line, a loop railway round Akari City, from the first train at dawn to the last train at night: stop exactly on the mark, keep the timetable to the second, and point and call every signal. Race up to three friends on the four-track Parallel Run.
aiHub.controls: Lever W/S or L2/R2 · Call E/✕ · Horn Space/□ · ATS Q/△ · EB Backspace/L1
